label: prf:sorting-color-energy
title: Proof of sorting color energy
html:
Proof. Sorting deposits energy because a disordered pair sits in the antisymmetric eigenspace at eigenvalue -q^{-1}, and sorting lifts it to the symmetric eigenspace at eigenvalue q; the exchange must therefore pay the gap between the two. We make this precise by computing the projections onto each eigenspace.

(1) The Hecke relation \sigma_i^2 - (q - q^{-1})\sigma_i - 1 = 0 has roots q and -q^{-1} by the quadratic formula. The corresponding idempotents are:

  e_+ = \frac{\sigma_i + q^{-1}}{q + q^{-1}}, \qquad
  e_- = \frac{q - \sigma_i}{q + q^{-1}}

with e_+ + e_- = 1 and e_+ e_- = 0. The image of e_+ is \mathrm{Sym}^2(V) (the symmetric representation, eigenvalue q); the image of e_- is \bigwedge^2(V) (the antisymmetric representation, eigenvalue -q^{-1}).

(2) A disordered pair occupies \bigwedge^2(V): the two items are in the wrong order, so the state is antisymmetric under exchange. Sorting swaps them into the correct order, moving the state to \mathrm{Sym}^2(V). This is the projection e_+. In the observation (observation), e_+ is the \mathrm{Ad} component: it acts on the colour fibre by conjugation, rotating the antisymmetric state to the symmetric eigenspace.

(3) The energy deposited is the eigenvalue difference: q - (-q^{-1}) = q + q^{-1}.

(4) Each adjacent transposition in the sorting algorithm corresponds to one braid crossing \sigma_i. The standard result from combinatorics: the minimum number of adjacent transpositions to realise \pi equals \mathrm{inv}(\pi), the number of pairs (i, j) with i < j and \pi(i) > \pi(j). Each crossing deposits q + q^{-1} in the colour fibre. \square

Example: three socks.

See Table.

At q = q_0: sorting three fully reversed socks costs 3 \times 2.011 = 6.033 action units in the colour fibre.
